newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ANZ says no comment on merger report.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ANZ says no comment on merger report.

text.p: The Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd (ANZ) said on Monday it had no comment to make on a newspaper report that ANZ and London-based Standard Chartered Plc were investigating a A$24 billion stock merger.
"We put that into the category of market speculation and so we won't be making a comment," ANZ spokesman David Wilson told Reuters.

A report in The Australian Financial Review earlier on Monday said that the two banks had engaged Goldman Sachs and Swiss Bank Corp to conduct a feasiblity study into a merger "along the lines of the RTZ-CRA stock stapling".
Asked if such a feasibility study was being carried out, Wilson said: "That's something that we're not in a position to comment on."
RTZ Corp Plc and CRA Ltd merged to become a dual-listed company and the world's biggest mining group in December last year.

A merged ANZ-Standard Chartered would have total market capitalisation of A$24 billion -- A$10 billion from ANZ and A$14 billion from Standard Chartered. Shareholders' funds would be A$9.5 billion, the newspaper said.

"Such an alliance would make ANZ almost takeover-proof in Australia, preserving the relative independence of one of the two major banks considered most likely takeover targets after the Wallis inquiry into the financial system," the report said.
ANZ and Standard Chartered both had been building extensive operations outside their core Australian and U.K. markets -- ANZ in Asia and the Middle East, Standard Chartered in Asia and Africa.

"There are no cross-shareholdings between ANZ and Standard Chartered and the issue of 'senior partner' in a stock stapling would be expected to be significant as would government and regulatory approval of the deal," the paper said.
ANZ had total assets of A$119.85 billion and net assets of A$6.05 billion as at March 31, 1996.
ANZ's share price closed 20 cents lower at A$7.16 on Friday, giving it a market capitalisation of A$10.58 billion. Standard Chartered closed up 26 pence at 6.78 stg on Friday.
The newspaper also said that KPMG, which audited both banks, had been taken on to perform due diligence.
